description:
Aquí en AstroCuy buscamos acercar toda la ciencia y preparación de un viaje espacial al publico en general de forma sencilla, asimilable y divertida.

Dividir el proceso en pequeñas partes progresivas para entender y desenredar la complejidad de la odisea que es realizar cada misión espacial.
summary: ORBITA is an educational browser game for designing and operating a complete CubeSat mission. Players choose a science objective, set measurable requirements, configure the spacecraft, select a compatible orbit and fictional launch vehicle, review the design and operate the mission until closure. Battery energy, memory and ground contacts connect engineering choices to mission outcomes. One to four participants can collaborate through local turns on a shared screen. A final report compares the outcome with the requirements and explains missed downlinks, memory overflow and energy limits. The game adapts mission-development concepts from NASA's CubeSat 101 using transparent, illustrative game parameters.
details:
### User experience

The game provides Coast Watch, Ice Watch and Radiation Mapper scenarios. Players specify a data target, minimum science quality, budget and mission lifetime. They choose a 3U or 6U platform, an optical camera, multispectral camera or dosimeter, a battery, solar panels and a radio. Regional and polar low-Earth-orbit options change the simplified sunlight and contact schedules. Three fictional launch vehicles impose different orbit and payload-mass constraints.

A preflight review checks instrument compatibility, quality, coverage, launcher compatibility, budget, mass, quantified requirements and crew validity. Every local participant must approve before launch. These are unauthenticated shared-screen game approvals, not digital signatures.

During operations, participants select capture, downlink or power-saving commands. Optical imaging requires sunlight, while the dosimeter can collect in eclipse. Data fill limited onboard memory and only count toward the objective after successful downlink during a scheduled contact. A scripted, optional power contingency asks the crew to choose between recalibration time and reduced generation. A mission succeeds only if it reaches its data target and survives to its planned end.

### Model and evaluation

The deterministic model advances internally in one-minute steps. Battery energy changes by `(solar generation - load) / 60` Wh per minute, bounded by battery capacity. The game also bounds memory, records discarded data and attributes commands to local participants. The score rewards science delivery, energy reserve and budget efficiency, with a collaboration component in team mode. The final report explains what happened and suggests changes based on the actual run.

One English prototype run delivered 132 MB against an 85 MB target, completed 192 simulated minutes and retained approximately 10.2 Wh. These are game results, not flight telemetry or evidence of measured learning outcomes.

### Implementation and limits

The prototype uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript without a required backend. It supports browser-local saving and JSON mission reports. Collaboration is local to one shared screen, not online multiplayer. Hardware, prices, power ratings, quality indices, orbital periods, eclipses and contacts are illustrative. The model does not propagate trajectories, calculate an RF link budget or simulate physical launch and disposal maneuvers. The project has no NASA affiliation or endorsement.

## Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

OpenAI Codex contributed to the initial concept, generated code, educational simulation rules, numerical game parameters, orbital SVG visualization, tests and documentation. CuyCorp selected and approved the proposed concept. The team supplied its logo and confirmed that it was generated or edited with AI. Visible AI labels accompany the logo and orbital visualization, and code and HTML metadata acknowledge AI assistance. The numerical game parameters are illustrative and are not NASA measurements. This disclosure includes assistance at the ideation stage; it does not by itself establish eligibility under the submission guide.

## NASA Data

We use NASA's CubeSat 101 as a conceptual educational resource, rather than a source of live telemetry or component values. Section 2.1, Concept Development, informs the objective-setting stage. Section 2.4, CubeSat Design, informs configuration of the spacecraft and its subsystems. Section 2.10, Ground Station Design, Development, and Testing, informs the learning concept that mission science must reach the ground station. Section 2.12, Mission Readiness Reviews, informs the preflight gate. Section 2.16, Mission Operations, informs command-based operations and mission closure. These are simplified game adaptations. Numerical costs, capacities, rates and contact schedules do not come from NASA.

Resource: https://science.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/nasa_csli_cubesat_101_508.pdf

## Space Agency Partner Data and Other References

No space-agency-partner dataset is currently integrated. Tools include JavaScript, HTML, CSS and OpenAI Codex. The CuyCorp team supplied its AI-generated or AI-edited logo. The orbital SVG is an AI-generated prototype illustration, not NASA imagery. Browser captures in the presentation show the actual English prototype. The team must include any additional resources it uses before submission and verify its rights to those materials.
